source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτά φησιν ὁ Ἰουδαῖος· πῶς δ᾿ ἐμέλλομεν τοῦτον νομίζειν θεὸν, ὃς τά τε ἄλλα. ὥσπερ ἐπηκούετο, οὐδὲν ὧν ἐπηγγέλλετο ἐπεδείκνυτο, καὶ ἐπειδὴ ἡμεῖς ἐλέγξαντες αὐτὸν καὶ καταγνόντες ἠξιοῦμεν κολάζεσθαι, κρυπτόμενος μὲν καὶ διαδιδράσκων ἐπονειδιστότατα ἑάλω, ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν δὲ ὧν ὠνόμαζε μαθητῶν προὐδόθη; καίτοι θεὸν. φησὶν. ὄντα οὔτε φεύγειν ἐνῆν οὔτε δεθέντα ἀπάγεσθαι. ἥκιστα δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν συνόντων αὐτῷ καὶ παντὸς ἰδίᾳ κεκοινωνηκότων καὶ διδασκάλῳ χρωμένων σωτῆρα νομιζόμενον καὶ θεοῦ τοῦ μεγίστου παῖδα καὶ ἄγγελον ἐγκαταλείπεσθαί τε καὶ ἐκδίδοσθαι. πρὸς ταῦτα δὲ φήσομεν ὅτι οὐδ᾿ ἡμεῖς ὑπολαμβάνομεν τὸ βλεπόμενον τότε καὶ αἰσθητὸν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ σῶμα εἶναι θεόν. καὶ τί λέγω τὸ σῶμα; ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ τὴν ψυχὴν, περὶ ἧς λέλεκται τό· „περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου.“ ἀλλ᾿ ὥσπερ κατὰ μὲν τὸν Ἰουδαίων λόγον ὁ λέγων· „ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ θεὸς πάσης σαρκὸς“ καὶ τό· „ἔμπροσθέν μου οὐκ ἐγένετο ἄλλος θεὸς. καὶ μετ᾿ ἐμὲ οὐκ ἔσται“ ὁ θεὸς εἶναι πεπίστευται, ὀργάνῳ τῇ ψυχῇ καὶ τῷ σώματι τοῦ προφήτου χρώμενος, κατὰ δὲ Ἕλληνας ὁ λέγων· οἶδα δ᾿ ἐγὼ ψάμμου τ᾿ ἀριθμὸν καὶ μέτρα θαλάσσης. καὶ κωφοῦ ξυνίημι, καὶ οὐ λαλέοντος ἀκούω θεὸς νενόμισται διὰ τῆς Πυθίας λέγων καὶ ἀκουόμενος· οὕτω καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς ὁ λόγος θεὸς καὶ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων υἱὸς ἔλεγεν ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ τό· „ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωὴ“ καὶ τό· „ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα“ καὶ τό· „ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ζῶν ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καταβὰς.“ καὶ εἴ τι ἄλλο τούτοις παραπλήσιον. ἐγκαλοῦμεν οὖν Ἰουδαίοις τοῦτον μὴ νομίσασι θεὸν, ὑπο τῶν προφητῶν πολλαχοῦ μεμαρτυρημένον ὡς μεγάλην ὄντα δύναμιν καὶ θεὸν κατὰ τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν καὶ πατέρα. τούτῳ γάρ φαμεν ἐν τῇ κατὰ Μωϋσέα κοσμοποιΐᾳ προστάττοντα τὸν πατέρα εἰρηκέναι τό· „γενηθήτω φῶς“ καὶ „γενηθήτω στερέωμα“ καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ, ὅσα προσέταξεν ὁ θεὸς γενέσθαι, καὶ τούτῳ εἰρηκέναι τό· „ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ᾿ εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμετέραν“· προσταχθέντα δὲ τὸν λόγον πεποιηκέναι πάντα, ὅσα ὁ πατὴρ αὐτῷ ἐνετείλατο. καὶ ταῦτα λέγομεν οὐκ αὐτοὶ ἐπιβάλλοντες ἀλλὰ ταῖς παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις φερομέναις προφητείαις πιστεύοντες· ἐν αἷς λέγεται περὶ θεοῦ καὶ τῶν δημιουργημάτων αὐταῖς λέξεσι τὰ οὕτως ἔχοντα· „ὅτι αὐτὸς εἶπε καὶ ἐγενήθησαν, αὐτὸς ἐνετείλατο καὶ ἐκτίσθησαν.“ εἰ γὰρ ἐνετείλατο ὁ θεὸς, καὶ ἐκτίσθη τὰ δημιουργήματα, τίς ἂν κατὰ τὸ ἀρέσκον τῷ προφητικῷ πνεύματι εἴη ὁ τὴν τηλικαύτην τοῦ πατρὸς ἐντολὴν ἐκπληρῶσαι δυνηθεὶς ἢ ὁ, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, ἔμψυχος λόγος καὶ „ἀλήθεια“ τυγχάνων; ὅτι δὲ τὸν ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ λέγοντα τό· „ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωὴ“ οὐδὲ τὰ εὐαγγέλια οἶδε περιγεγραμμένον τινὰ γεγονέναι, ὡς οὐδαμοῦ ἔξω τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τυγχάνοντα, δῆλον μὲν καὶ ἀπὸ πολλῶν καὶ ἐξ ὀλίγων δὲ ὧν παραθησόμεθα οὕτως ἐχόντων. ὁ βαπτιστὴς Ἰωάννης προφητεύων ὅσον οὐδέπω ἐνστήσεσθαι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ, οὐκ ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ σώματι καὶ τῇ ψυχῇ τυγχάνοντα ἀλλὰ γὰρ φθάνοντα πανταχοῦ, λέγει περὶ αὐτοῦ· „μέσος ὑμῶν στήκει, ὃν ὑμεῖς οὐκ οἴδατε, ὀπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος.“ εἴπερ οὖν ἐνόει ἐκεῖ μόνον εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅπου τὸ βλεπόμενον ἦν σῶμα Ἰησοῦ, πῶς ἔφασκεν ἂν τό· „μέσος ὑμῶν στήκει, ὃν ὑμεῖς οὐκ οἴδατε“; καὶ αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐπαίρων τὸ φρόνημα τῶν μαθητευόντων αὐτῷ εἰς τὸ μείζονα φρονεῖν περὶ υἱοῦ θεοῦ φησιν· „ὅπου δύο ἢ τρεῖς συνηγμένοι εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα, ἐκεῖ εἰμι ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν.“ τοιαύτη δ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἐστι καὶ ἡ πρὸς τοὺς μαθητὰς ἐπαγγελία λέγοντος· „καὶ ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ μεθ᾿ ὑμῶν εἰμι πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας ἕως τῆς συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος.“ ταῦτα δέ φαμεν οὐ χωρίζοντες τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ· ἓν γὰρ μάλιστα μετὰ τὴν οἰκονομίαν γεγένηται πρὸς τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τὸ σῶμα Ἰησοῦ. εἰ γὰρ κατὰ τὴν Παύλου διδασκαλίαν λέγοντος· „ὁ κολλώμενος τῷ κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστι“ πᾶς ὁ νοήσας, τί τὸ κολλᾶσθαι τῷ κυρίῳ, καὶ κολληθεὶς αὐτῷ ἕν ἐστι πνεῦμα πρὸς τὸν κύριον, πῶς οὐ πολλῷ μᾶλλον θειοτέρως καὶ μειζόνως ἕν ἐστι τό ποτε σύνθετον πρὸς τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ; οὗτος δὴ ἐπεδείξατο ἐν Ἰουδαίοις „θεοῦ δύναμις“ ὢν τὸ τοιοῦτον δι᾿ ὧν παραδόξων ἐποίησεν, ὑπονοηθέντων ὑπὸ μὲν Κέλσου γοητείᾳ γεγονέναι ὑπὸ δὲ τῶν τότε Ἰουδαίων, οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὁπόθεν τὰ περὶ Βεελζεβοὺλ μεμαθηκότων, „ἐν Βεελζεβοὺλ. ἄρχοντι τῶν δαιμονίων,“ ἐκβάλλειν „τὰ δαιμόνια.“ οὓς ἤλεγξεν ἀτοπώτατα λέγοντας ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν ἐκεῖ τῷ μηδέπω τέλος ἔχειν τὴν τῆς κακίας βασιλείαν· ὅπερ ἔσται δῆλον τοῖς φρονίμως ἐντυγχάνουσι τῇ εὐαγγελικῇ γραφῇ, ἣν οὐ καιρὸς νῦν διηγήσασθαι.
pass_a_gloss: After these things the Jew says: 'How were we to think (νομίζειν) this one God (θεός), who both in the other things, as was heard (ἐπηκούετο), showed (ἐπεδείκνυτο) none of the things he promised (ἐπηγγέλλετο), and when we, having convicted (ἐλέγξαντες) and condemned (καταγνόντες) him, thought it right (ἠξιοῦμεν) that he be punished, hiding (κρυπτόμενος) and running away (διαδιδράσκων) was caught (ἑάλω) most disgracefully (ἐπονειδιστότατα), and was betrayed (προὐδόθη) by the very ones he named disciples?' 'And yet,' he says, 'being God, it was possible neither to flee nor, bound, to be led away (ἀπάγεσθαι); and least of all, being thought a saviour (σωτήρ) and child (παῖς) and angel/messenger (ἄγγελος) of the greatest God, to be abandoned (ἐγκαταλείπεσθαι) and handed over (ἐκδίδοσθαι) by those with him and having shared everything privately and using him as teacher.' To these we will say that neither do we suppose the then-seen and perceptible (αἰσθητόν) body of Jesus to be God. And why do I say the body? But not even the soul (ψυχή), about which was said: 'My soul is very grieved (περίλυπος) to death.' But as according to the Jews' account the one saying 'I [am the] Lord, the God of all flesh' and 'Before me there came to be no other god, and after me there will not be' has been believed to be God, using as an instrument (ὄργανον) the soul and body of the prophet; and according to Greeks the one saying 'I know the number of the sand and the measures of the sea, and I understand the dumb (κωφός), and hear the one not speaking' has been considered a god, speaking and being heard through the Pythia: so according to us the Word (λόγος), God (θεός, anarthrous) and son of the God of the universe (τῶν ὅλων), spoke in Jesus: 'I am the way and the truth and the life', and 'I am the door', and 'I am the living bread that came down from heaven', and anything else similar. We accuse (ἐγκαλοῦμεν), then, the Jews for not having thought him God, borne witness to (μεμαρτυρημένον) in many places by the prophets as being a great power (δύναμις) and God according to (κατά) the God and Father of the universe. For to him, we say, in the world-making (κοσμοποιΐα) according to Moses, the Father commanding (προστάττοντα) said 'Let light come to be' and 'Let a firmament (στερέωμα) come to be' and the rest God commanded to come to be, and to him said 'Let us make man according to our image (εἰκών) and likeness (ὁμοίωσις)'; and the Word, being commanded, made all the Father enjoined (ἐνετείλατο) him. And these things we say not ourselves imposing/conjecturing (ἐπιβάλλοντες) but believing the prophecies current (φερομέναις) among the Jews, in which it is said about God and the created works (δημιουργήματα) in the very words (αὐταῖς λέξεσι) as follows: 'For he spoke and they came to be, he commanded and they were created (ἐκτίσθησαν).' For if God commanded and the works were created, who, according to what pleases (κατὰ τὸ ἀρέσκον) the prophetic spirit (προφητικὸν πνεῦμα), would be the one able to fulfil (ἐκπληρῶσαι) so great a command (ἐντολή) of the Father, except the one who is, so to name him, the ensouled/living Word (ἔμψυχος λόγος) and 'truth'? That the Gospels too do not know the one saying in Jesus 'I am the way and the truth and the life' to have been someone circumscribed (περιγεγραμμένον), as being nowhere outside the soul and body of Jesus, is clear from many things and also from a few we shall set beside (παραθησόμεθα) as follows. The Baptist John, prophesying that the Son of God would very soon (ὅσον οὐδέπω) be present (ἐνστήσεσθαι), not being in that body and soul but reaching (φθάνοντα) everywhere, says about him: 'In the midst of you stands one whom you do not know, coming after me.' If then he thought the Son of God to be only there where the seen body of Jesus was, how would he say 'In the midst of you stands one whom you do not know'? And Jesus himself, raising the mind (φρόνημα) of his disciples to thinking greater things (μείζονα φρονεῖν) about the Son of God, says: 'Where two or three are gathered into my name, there I am in their midst.' Such too is his promise (ἐπαγγελία) to the disciples, saying: 'And behold, I am with you all the days until the consummation of the age (συντέλεια τοῦ αἰῶνος).' These things we say not separating (χωρίζοντες) the Son of God from Jesus; for one (ἕν) most of all after the dispensation (οἰκονομία) have become, with the Word of God, the soul and body of Jesus. For if, according to the teaching of Paul saying 'He who is joined (κολλώμενος) to the Lord is one spirit', everyone who has understood what being joined to the Lord is, and having been joined to him, is one spirit with the Lord, how not much more, more divinely (θειοτέρως) and greatly, is the once-composite thing (τό ποτε σύνθετον) one with the Word of God? This one indeed showed among Jews that he was such, 'power of God', through the wonders (παράδοξα) he did, suspected by Celsus to have come about by sorcery (γοητεία), but by the Jews of then, who had learned from I know not where the things about Beelzebul, [suspected] to cast out 'the demons' 'by Beelzebul, ruler (ἄρχων) of the demons'; whom our Saviour (σωτήρ) refuted there as saying most absurd things, by the kingdom of wickedness (κακία) not yet having an end (τέλος); which will be clear to those reading the Gospel scripture prudently (φρονίμως), which it is not the time now to recount.
pass_b_english: After this the Jew says: “How could we have regarded as God one who, among other things, as was commonly heard, displayed none of what he promised; and who, when we had convicted and condemned him and judged that he should be punished, was caught hiding and running away in the most disgraceful way, and was betrayed by the very men he called his disciples? And yet,” he says, “one who was God could neither flee nor be bound and led away; and least of all could one who was thought to be a saviour, and son and angel of the greatest God, be deserted and handed over by those who were with him, who had shared everything with him privately, and who had him for their teacher.”

To this we shall say that we too do not suppose that the body of Jesus, which was then seen and perceived by the senses, was God. And why do I speak of the body? Not even his soul, of which it is said: “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38; Mark 14:34). But just as, according to the Jews’ account, he who says “I am the Lord, the God of all flesh” (Jeremiah 32:27) and “Before me there was no other god, and after me there will be none” (Isaiah 43:10) is believed to be God, using the soul and body of the prophet as an instrument; and as, according to the Greeks, he who says “I know the number of the sand and the measures of the sea; I understand the mute, and I hear one who does not speak” (Herodotus, Histories 1.47) is held to be a god, speaking and being heard through the Pythia; so, according to us, the Word, who is God and Son of the God of the universe, said in Jesus: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6), and “I am the door” (John 10:9), and “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51), and anything else like these.

We therefore charge the Jews with not regarding him as God, though the prophets in many places bear witness that he is a great power, and God in accordance with the God and Father of the universe. For we say that it was to him that the Father gave the command in the creation of the world recorded by Moses, saying “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3) and “Let there be a firmament” (Genesis 1:6), and all the rest that God commanded to come into being; and that it was to him he said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26); and that the Word, so commanded, made all that the Father enjoined on him. We say this not as our own conjecture, but because we believe the prophecies current among the Jews, in which these very words are said about God and the things he made: “For he spoke, and they came into being; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 33:9; Psalm 148:5). For if God commanded and the things made were created, who, in the mind of the prophetic Spirit, could be the one able to carry out so great a command of the Father, except he who is, if I may so name him, the living Word and “the Truth” (John 14:6)?

That the Gospels too do not know the one who said in Jesus “I am the way and the truth and the life” as someone circumscribed, as though he existed nowhere outside the soul and body of Jesus, is plain from many passages, and also from the few that we shall cite, which run as follows. John the Baptist, prophesying that the Son of God would very soon appear, not as one confined to that body and soul but as one who reaches everywhere, says of him: “Among you stands one whom you do not know, who comes after me” (John 1:26–27). If, then, he had thought that the Son of God was only where the visible body of Jesus was, how could he have said, “Among you stands one whom you do not know”? And Jesus himself, raising the thoughts of his disciples to think greater things about the Son of God, says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am among them” (Matthew 18:20). Of the same kind is his promise to the disciples when he says: “And behold, I am with you all the days until the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

We say this without separating the Son of God from Jesus; for after the saving dispensation the soul and body of Jesus have become, in the fullest sense, one with the Word of God. For if, according to the teaching of Paul, who says, “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17), everyone who has understood what it is to be joined to the Lord, and has been joined to him, is one spirit with the Lord, how much more, in a more divine and greater way, is that which was once composite one with the Word of God? He indeed showed among the Jews that he was “the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24) by the wonders he worked. Celsus suspected that these were done by sorcery; the Jews of that time, who had learned the tales about Beelzebul from I know not where, suspected that he cast out “demons by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons” (Matthew 12:24; Mark 3:22; Luke 11:15). Our Saviour refuted them there for speaking most absurdly, by pointing out that the kingdom of evil had not yet come to an end (Matthew 12:26; Mark 3:26). This will be clear to those who read the Gospel scripture with understanding; but this is not the time to explain it.

choices.why: 'after the Incarnation' -> 'after the saving dispensation' (οἰκονομία; 'Incarnation' narrowed a doctrinal term Origen may use of the completed saving work).
'as people heard' -> 'as was commonly heard' (ὥσπερ ἐπηκούετο; smoother, same sense).
'not as something we impose on the text ourselves' -> 'not as our own conjecture' (ἐπιβάλλοντες; 'on the text' was added).

Checked LXX numbering: Jeremiah 39:27 LXX = 32:27, Psalm 32:9 LXX = 33:9, Psalm 148:5; Isaiah 43:10, Matthew 26:38, Mark 14:34, John 14:6, 10:9, 6:51, Genesis 1:3, 1:6, 1:26, John 1:26-27, Matthew 18:20, 28:20, 1 Corinthians 6:17, 1:24, Beelzebul passages and Herodotus 1.47 confirmed.

2.9 κατὰ τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν καὶ πατέρα: kept as the literal 'in accordance with', noted as open ('second to' / 'deriving from'); no owner action needed

translator_notes: Celsus’s Jew speaks in direct speech (first person plural) and is quoted; the stray full stops in the staged text after ἄλλα and around φησίν are treated as commas. ὥσπερ ἐπηκούετο (‘as people heard’) is compressed: it may mean ‘as was reported of him’ or ‘as he was heeded’. ἄγγελον is rendered ‘angel’ (it can also mean ‘messenger’); σωτῆρα in the Jew’s mouth is lower case, ‘a saviour’. LXX renumbering: Jeremiah 39:27 LXX = Jeremiah 32:27 English (ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ θεὸς πάσης σαρκός); Psalm 32:9 LXX = Psalm 33:9 English. The words ‘he spoke and they came into being; he commanded and they were created’ stand identically in LXX Psalm 32:9 and LXX Psalm 148:5 (the Hebrew of 148:5 lacks ‘he spoke and they came into being’), so both are cited. Isaiah 43:10 agrees with the LXX. Genesis 1:26: Origen’s wording ‘according to our image and likeness’ compresses the LXX κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν. The Pythian verses are the Delphic oracle to Croesus in Herodotus 1.47 (certain); θεός there is lower case because it is Apollo. ὁ λόγος θεός: θεός is anarthrous, as Origen uses it of the Word; rendered ‘the Word, who is God’. κατὰ τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν καὶ πατέρα rendered literally ‘in accordance with the God and Father of the universe’; it may mean ‘second to’ or ‘deriving from’; no interpretation is imposed. ἔμψυχος λόγος, literally ‘ensouled Word’, rendered ‘living Word’; Origen himself flags the term (ἵν’ οὕτως ὀνομάσω). οὐκ ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ σώματι ... τυγχάνοντα, literally ‘not being in that body and soul’, rendered ‘not as one confined to’, since the contrast is with φθάνοντα πανταχοῦ and περιγεγραμμένον; Origen does not deny that the Word was in Jesus (see the next paragraph). οἰκονομία rendered ‘the saving dispensation’: Origen may mean the Incarnation or its completion in the Passion and Resurrection, so the term is not narrowed. ἐπιβάλλοντες rendered ‘as our own conjecture’ (putting a thing forward on one’s own); contrasted with belief in the prophecies. John 1:26-27: Origen reads στήκει for ἕστηκεν. The Saviour’s reply (Matthew 12:25-26; Mark 3:23-26) is summarised by Origen: Mark 3:26 has τέλος ἔχει (‘has an end’), which his τέλος ἔχειν echoes. ‘The prophetic Spirit’ is capitalised as the Holy Spirit.
